- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- simplify: Review changed code for reuse, quality, and efficiency, then fix any issues found.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled remote agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring remote agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. Also use when the user wants a one-time scheduled run ("run this once at 3pm", "remind me to check X tomorrow").
- claude-api: Build, debug, and optimize Claude API / Anthropic SDK apps. Apps built with this skill should include prompt caching. Also handles migrating existing Claude API code between Claude model versions (4.5 → 4.6, 4.6 → 4.7, retired-model replacements).
TRIGGER when: code imports `anthropic`/`@anthropic-ai/sdk`; user asks for the Claude API, Anthropic SDK, or Managed Agents; user adds/modifies/tunes a Claude feature (caching, thinking, compaction, tool use, batch, files, citations, memory) or model (Opus/Sonnet/Haiku) in a file; questions about prompt caching / cache hit rate in an Anthropic SDK project.
SKIP: file imports `openai`/other-provider SDK, filename like `*-openai.py`/`*-generic.py`, provider-neutral code, general programming/ML.
- init: Initialize a new CLAUDE.md file with codebase documentation
- review: Review a pull request
- security-review: Complete a security review of the pending changes on the current branch

# Writing Plan — provenance_weight_training

# Contract for downstream writing Workers

venue: EMNLP 2026 ARR May 25
deadline: 2026-05-25
page_limit: 8 (+ unlimited appendix)

title: "Minimum Intervention Reweighting: Adaptive Exponent Selection for Contamination-Aware Pretraining"
# 备选:
# - "Dual-Constrained Adaptive Reweighting for Pretraining on Contaminated Web Corpora"
# - "How Much to Downweight? Principled Exponent Selection for Contamination-Aware Pretraining"

abstract_outline:
  - sentence_1: "Web pretraining corpora contain 20–60% machine-generated text of unknown provenance, and naive training on such mixtures degrades model quality (model collapse)."
  - sentence_2: "Existing detect-and-reweight methods (Drayson et al., 2025) require per-model validation-based grid search over the weighting exponent b, which is expensive and fragile."
  - sentence_3: "We propose a dual-constrained adaptive b* that jointly enforces a quality lower bound (α_eff ≥ τ) and a stability upper bound (ESS ≥ n_min), yielding the minimum intervention—the smallest b that achieves sufficient cleaning per batch, with zero validation cost."
  - sentence_4: "On FineWeb with Qwen3-0.6B, adaptive b* matches grid-search-optimal performance within seed variance while eliminating 6× search cost, and outperforms both uniform training and the max-intervention (ESS-only) baseline."

# ============================================================
# SECTIONS
# ============================================================

sections:

  introduction:
    target_pages: 1.0
    key_points:
      - "Web corpora contamination is pervasive (20–60%) and growing; strong model collapse occurs even at low contamination (Dohmatob et al., 2025)"
      - "Detect-and-reweight via w=(1-q)^b is effective (Drayson et al., 2025), but b selection requires per-model validation grid search"
      - "Problem statement: given per-sample detector scores q, how to choose b without validation?"
      - "Our answer: dual-constrained adaptive b* — α_eff(b) ≥ τ (quality floor) + ESS(b) ≥ n_min (stability ceiling) → minimum intervention principle"
      - "Key insight: α_eff monotonically increasing, ESS monotonically decreasing → b has a lower bound b_τ and upper bound b_ESS; b* = b_τ when feasible"
    contributions:
      - "Dual-constrained framework for adaptive b* selection with minimum intervention semantics (Section 3)"
      - "Empirical demonstration that adaptive b* matches grid-best within seed variance at zero validation cost (Section 5)"
      - "Evidence that minimum intervention (dual-constraint) outperforms maximum intervention (ESS-only), and that a lightweight TF-IDF+LR detector suffices (Section 5)"
    evidence:
      - adaptive_fix_seed42
      - adaptive_fix_seed123
      - adaptive_fix_seed456
      - ess_only_seed42

  related_work:
    target_pages: 1.0
    groups:
      synthetic_contamination_and_collapse:
        narrative: "Model collapse under recursive/contaminated training"
        papers:
          - shumailov_2024_model_collapse

Golden Ratio~\citep{he2025golden} achieves 17.654 (seed\,42), comparable to adaptive $\bstar$ at 17.653 on the same seed, despite requiring oracle access to the true contamination ratio $\rho$.

Detect \& Remove at its best threshold ($q{>}0.3$) achieves 3-seed mean PPL $17.250 \pm 0.001$ at full training length, apparently outperforming all reweighting methods by a wide margin.
However, filtering retains only 31.5\% of tokens, so the model sees surviving data ${\sim}$3.2 \emph{content epochs} (times each unique document is seen) versus one for reweighting.
An epoch-matched control (training D\&R at $q{>}0.5$ for 2{,}533 steps to equalize content epochs at ${\sim}$1.0) yields 3-seed mean PPL $17.657 \pm 0.006$, within 0.006 of adaptive $\bstar$ ($17.651 \pm 0.007$); the entire advantage of full-length D\&R is attributable to multi-epoch exposure, not to filtering itself (Table~\ref{tab:epoch_match}).
D\&R also demands threshold calibration: raw PPL traces a U-shaped curve ($q{>}0.1$: 17.40, $q{>}0.3$: 17.25, $q{>}0.9$: 17.42), suggesting an optimal threshold near $q{>}0.3$.
However, epoch-matched comparisons eliminate the U-shape entirely, revealing monotonically decreasing PPL that saturates near the adaptive level at $q{\geq}0.5$ (Figure~\ref{fig:dr_dual_curve}, Appendix~\ref{app:hybrid}).
The apparent optimum at $q{>}0.3$ is not a genuine quality threshold; it is the point where multi-epoch exposure happens to compensate maximally for the information loss from filtering.

As synthetic text reaches an estimated 20--60\% of web corpora, detect-and-reweight methods that downweight likely-synthetic samples via $w(x) = (1-q(x))^b$ have gained traction.
Two questions remain open: does hard filtering outperform soft reweighting, and how should the exponent $b$ be set without per-model grid search?

Through controlled experiments (Qwen3-0.6B continued pretraining, 132M FineWeb tokens, 40\% contamination, 3 seeds), we identify two confounds in current evaluation practice.
Detect and Remove (D\&R) owes its reported advantage entirely to multi-epoch exposure: at matched content epochs, D\&R and reweighting differ by only 0.006 perplexity ($N{=}3$).
In-distribution perplexity gains from adaptive reweighting do not transfer out-of-distribution (OpenWebText $+$0.06, Wikipedia $+$0.14), consistent with distribution matching rather than general quality improvement.
A dual-constrained adaptive $b^*$, selecting the minimum exponent that satisfies a quality floor while preserving gradient stability, matches grid-search performance without per-model tuning (gap 0.031, within seed variance $\pm$0.033); detector signal type appears to matter more than discrimination accuracy (3 detectors, single seed).
The method fails at $\rho{=}0.2$ and shows no effect at 1.7B; with $N{=}3$, we report effect sizes and directional consistency rather than formal significance.

\paragraph{Training Data.}
We sample a 132M-token subset of FineWeb~\citep{penedo2024fineweb} as the real-data source, comparable to typical domain-adaptive continued pretraining budgets~\citep{gururangan2020dont}.
To simulate web-scale synthetic contamination, we generate continuations with Qwen3-0.6B~\citep{yang2025qwen3}, the same architecture used for continued pretraining, and inject them at token-level ratio $\rho = 0.4$ via uniform random mixing.\footnote{$\rho$ denotes the token-level contamination ratio. Because synthetic documents are shorter on average (304 vs.\ 560 words), the document-level synthetic fraction is 55.6\% at $\rho{=}0.4$.}
This self-contamination design means generator and trainee share the same distribution; implications for detection difficulty are discussed in \S\ref{sec:limitations}.

\paragraph{Detector.}
We train a TF-IDF + Logistic Regression classifier on a held-out labeled split (AUC\,=\,0.939, calibrated ECE\,=\,0.048 after temperature scaling with $T = 0.204$).
The resulting $q$-scores have mean 0.60, standard deviation 0.37, and median 0.71, with 46.3\% of samples in the uncertain range $[0.2, 0.8]$.
We use this lightweight detector rather than neural alternatives (e.g., ModernBERT at AUC\,${\geq}$\,0.98 in \citealt{drayson2025detection}) to test whether score \emph{calibration} may matter as much as raw discrimination for reweighting.
To evaluate detector sensitivity, we additionally test two generative baselines: a GPT-2-based perplexity scorer (AUC\,=\,0.913) and an N-gram language model perplexity scorer (AUC\,=\,0.73); results are reported in \S\ref{sec:robustness}.

\paragraph{Training.}
We continue pretraining Qwen3-0.6B from its pretrained weights for 6{,}103 steps (batch size 4, gradient accumulation 4, effective batch 16) with AdamW, cosine schedule (peak lr\,=\,$5{\times}10^{-5}$), max sequence length 2048, and bf16 precision on a single NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 (96\,GB).
All main comparisons use three random seeds (42, 123, 456).

\paragraph{Evaluation.}
We report held-out perplexity (PPL) on a held-out subset of FineWeb (67.8K documents, $\sim$4M tokens) containing only human-authored text, via sliding-window evaluation (stride 1024).
All evaluations are post-hoc with a unified pipeline; training involves no inline evaluation.

\paragraph{Methods.}
We compare six approaches:
\begin{itemize}[nosep,leftmargin=*]
  \item \textbf{Uniform}: $w_j = 1$ for all $j$ (no contamination handling).
  \item \textbf{Grid-$b$}: fixed $b \in \{0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.5, 1.0, 1.5, 2.0, 3.0, 5.0\}$ (nine candidates), best selected post-hoc by held-out PPL.
        Represents validation-based selection~\citep{drayson2025detection}.
  \item \textbf{ESS-only}: $b^* = \max\{b : \mathrm{ESS}(b) \geq n_{\min}\}$, the maximum-intervention variant retaining only the stability constraint, ablating $\alpha_{\mathrm{eff}}$.
  \item \textbf{Golden Ratio}: $w = 1/\varphi \approx 0.618$ for synthetic ($q_j > 0.5$), $w = 1$ otherwise~\citep{he2025golden}.
        Requires known provenance labels (oracle).
  \item \textbf{Adaptive} (ours): per-batch $b^*$ from the dual-constraint formulation (\S\ref{sec:method}), with $\tau = 0.8$ and $n_{\min} = 2$ (half the micro-batch size).
  \item \textbf{Detect \& Remove}: hard filtering that discards samples with $q_j > 0.5$ and trains uniformly on the remainder.
        Requires a calibrated detection threshold; threshold sensitivity is analyzed in \S\ref{sec:main-results}.
\end{itemize}

4	Table~\ref{tab:main} reports held-out perplexity at $\rho = 0.4$ across three seeds.
5	Continued pretraining reduces PPL from 22.970 (pretrained checkpoint) to the 17.3--17.8 range; the initial 5.2-point drop absorbs the bulk of easy gains, and reweighting method comparisons operate within a narrow residual.

7	Adaptive $\bstar$ achieves 3-seed mean PPL 17.651, compared to 17.620 for grid $b{=}0.3$ (gap 0.031, 95\% CI $[-0.039, 0.101]$, which includes possible degradation).
8	With only $N{=}3$ seeds, normality cannot be verified; we report exact per-seed gaps (0.013, 0.064, 0.017) and note lower cross-seed variance ($\pm$0.007 vs.\ $\pm$0.033).
9	The practical value is reducing $b$ grid search from nine full training runs to one~\citep{drayson2025detection}, saving ${\sim}$16 GPU-hours at 0.6B scale.
10	The grid-best $b{=}0.3$ is a post-hoc oracle selected after observing all nine candidates; in practice, validation-based selection from the same grid would yield worse results due to the noisy PPL plateau at $b \in [0.1, 0.5]$ (Figure~\ref{fig:grid_b_trend}).

14	Random weights $\mathcal{U}(0,2)$ (mean 17.802) perform worse than uniform (17.694): the detector's $q$-scores carry genuine provenance information, and uninformed reweighting increases gradient variance without corrective signal.

\subsection{Main Results}
\label{sec:main-results}

Table~\ref{tab:main} reports held-out perplexity at $\rho = 0.4$ across three seeds.
Continued pretraining reduces PPL from 22.970 (pretrained checkpoint) to the 17.3--17.8 range; the initial 5.2-point drop absorbs the bulk of easy gains, and reweighting method comparisons operate within a narrow residual.

Adaptive $\bstar$ achieves 3-seed mean PPL 17.651, compared to 17.620 for grid $b{=}0.3$ (gap 0.031, 95\% CI $[-0.039, 0.101]$, which includes possible degradation).
With only $N{=}3$ seeds, normality cannot be verified; we report exact per-seed gaps (0.013, 0.064, 0.017) and note lower cross-seed variance ($\pm$0.007 vs.\ $\pm$0.033).
The practical value is reducing $b$ grid search from nine full training runs to one~\citep{drayson2025detection}, saving ${\sim}$16 GPU-hours at 0.6B scale.
The grid-best $b{=}0.3$ is a post-hoc oracle selected after observing all nine candidates; in practice, validation-based selection from the same grid would yield worse results due to the noisy PPL plateau at $b \in [0.1, 0.5]$ (Figure~\ref{fig:grid_b_trend}).
At the grid point nearest mean per-batch $\bstar$ ($b{=}1.0$, seed\,42), PPL is 17.692, indistinguishable from uniform (17.694); per-batch adaptation is essential.

The ablation hierarchy at $\rho{=}0.4$ (Adaptive ${<}$ Uniform ${<}$ ESS-only ${<}$ Random, Table~\ref{tab:main}) reveals two requirements for effective reweighting: detector signal and minimum intervention.
Random weights $\mathcal{U}(0,2)$ (mean 17.802) perform worse than uniform (17.694): the detector's $q$-scores carry genuine provenance information, and uninformed reweighting increases gradient variance without corrective signal.
ESS-only (mean $17.738 {\pm} 0.022$) uses the same $q$-scores but maximizes $b$ up to the stability ceiling, concentrating weights on a few high-confidence samples; it provides no improvement over uniform.
Only the dual-constrained adaptive method, which limits $b$ to the minimum needed, improves in-distribution PPL over uniform (paired $\Delta$: $-$0.041, $-$0.043, $-$0.045; mean $-$0.043, directionally consistent across all seeds; $N{=}3$ precludes formal significance testing).
Figure~\ref{fig:grid_b_trend} contextualizes this: the grid curve has a broad plateau at $b \in [0.1, 0.5]$ (PPL 17.620--17.655), and adaptive $\bstar$ (mean 17.651) falls within it; ESS-only $\bstar$ (mean 3.5--5.9) lies in the degradation zone beyond the plateau.

Golden Ratio~\citep{he2025golden} achieves 17.654 (seed\,42), comparable to adaptive $\bstar$ at 17.653 on the same seed, despite requiring oracle access to the true contamination ratio $\rho$.

\paragraph{Hard filtering and the epoch confound.}
Detect \& Remove at its best threshold ($q{>}0.3$) achieves 3-seed mean PPL $17.250 \pm 0.001$ at full training length, apparently outperforming all reweighting methods by a wide margin.
However, filtering retains only 31.5\% of tokens, so the model sees surviving data ${\sim}$3.2 \emph{content epochs} (times each unique document is seen) versus one for reweighting.
An epoch-matched control (training D\&R at $q{>}0.5$ for 2{,}533 steps to equalize content epochs at ${\sim}$1.0) yields 3-seed mean PPL $17.657 \pm 0.006$, within 0.006 of adaptive $\bstar$ ($17.651 \pm 0.007$); the entire advantage of full-length D\&R is attributable to multi-epoch exposure, not to filtering itself (Table~\ref{tab:epoch_match}).
D\&R also demands threshold calibration: raw PPL traces a U-shaped curve ($q{>}0.1$: 17.40, $q{>}0.3$: 17.25, $q{>}0.9$: 17.42), suggesting an optimal threshold near $q{>}0.3$.
However, epoch-matched comparisons eliminate the U-shape entirely, revealing monotonically decreasing PPL that saturates near the adaptive level at $q{\geq}0.5$ (Figure~\ref{fig:dr_dual_curve}, Appendix~\ref{app:hybrid}).
The apparent optimum at $q{>}0.3$ is not a genuine quality threshold; it is the point where multi-epoch exposure happens to compensate maximally for the information loss from filtering.

4	\begin{proposition}[$\alpha_{\mathrm{eff}}$ monotonicity]
5	\label{prop:monotone}

9	\begin{proof}[Proof of Proposition~\ref{prop:monotone}]
10	Let $w_i(b) = (1 - q_i)^b$, $W(b) = \sum_{j=1}^B w_j(b)$, and $\pi_i(b) = w_i(b) / W(b)$.
11	Then
12	\begin{equation*}
13	  \alpha_{\mathrm{eff}}(b) = \sum_{i=1}^{B} \pi_i(b)\, r_i,
14	\end{equation*}
15	where $r_i \in \{0, 1\}$ indicates whether sample $i$ is real.
16	Taking the derivative with respect to $b$:
17	\begin{align*}
18	  \frac{d\pi_i}{db}
19	  &= \pi_i \!\left(\frac{d \ln w_i}{db} - \frac{d \ln W}{db}\right)
20	  = \pi_i \!\left(\ln(1{-}q_i) - \sum_j \pi_j \ln(1{-}q_j)\right).

26	  &= \mathrm{Cov}_{\pi}\!\bigl(r_i,\, \ln(1{-}q_i)\bigr).

An alternative, Detect and Remove (D\&R), hard-filters samples above a threshold~\citep{feng2025beyond}.

Despite growing adoption, fundamental questions remain.
Does D\&R genuinely outperform soft reweighting, or do published comparisons confound filtering quality with multi-epoch exposure?
How should $b$ be chosen, given that \citet{drayson2025detection} find optimal values ranging from $b{=}10$ (GPT-2 124M) to $b{=}1$ (SmolLM 1.7B), requiring costly per-model grid search?
What detector properties are necessary for effective reweighting?

We investigate these questions through controlled experiments on Qwen3-0.6B continued pretraining (132M FineWeb tokens, $\rho{=}0.4$, 3 seeds), with extensions to $\rho \in \{0.2, 0.6\}$ and 1.7B parameters.\footnote{Our scope is continued pretraining on moderate-scale corpora with known contamination~\citep{gururangan2020dont}; generalization to from-scratch pretraining at web scale is untested.}
For the exponent selection problem, we derive $b$ per-batch from a dual-constrained formulation: find the minimum $b$ such that the weighted effective real proportion $\alpha_{\mathrm{eff}}(b) \geq \tau$ (quality floor, motivated by convergence theory~\citep{wang2026survive}), subject to Kish's effective sample size $\mathrm{ESS}(b) \geq n_{\min}$ (stability ceiling)~\citep{kish1965survey,vehtari2024psis}.

Our analysis identifies two evaluation confounds and characterizes adaptive reweighting:
\begin{itemize}[nosep,leftmargin=*]
\item \textbf{Epoch confound.}

1	\paragraph{Why minimum intervention works.}
2	The $\aeff$ constraint prevents 4.9$\times$ over-aggressive downweighting in 38.2\% of batches (\S\ref{sec:regime}), with consistent behavior across $\rho$ and seeds (CV ${<}2\%$).
3	A fixed exponent at the aggregate mean $\bstar$ ($b{=}1.0$) yields PPL 17.692, indistinguishable from uniform (17.694): per-batch adaptation is essential, and the minimum intervention principle (adaptive, 17.651) outperforms maximum intervention (ESS-only, 17.738).
4	
5	\paragraph{Failure modes and applicability boundary.}
6	At $\rho{=}0.2$, the method degrades by $+$0.046 PPL (Appendix~\ref{app:rho02}): the detector's mean $q$-score drops to 0.393, yet $\aeff$-binding rises to 60.1\%, so the method actively intervenes on unreliable signal.
7	The same pattern appears with generative detectors (GPT-2 PPL: $\Delta{=}{+}0.10$; N-gram PPL: $\Delta{=}{+}0.13$), which conflate predictability with provenance.
8	Both failure modes share a common root cause: when $q$-scores do not separate real from synthetic, the framework amplifies detector error rather than correcting for contamination.
9	The effective range with $\tau{=}0.8$ requires discriminative signal and $\rho \geq 0.4$.
10	
11	\paragraph{Distribution matching, not quality gain.}
12	The in-distribution PPL improvement reverses out-of-distribution ($+$0.06 OpenWebText, $+$0.14 Wikipedia; seed 42, other-seed checkpoints not retained), consistent with distribution matching rather than general improvement.
13	This pattern likely affects all contamination-aware reweighting that upweights human-authored samples~\citep{drayson2025detection}: in-distribution PPL may be an inadequate metric for evaluating contamination mitigation, since any method that shifts the training distribution toward the evaluation distribution will show gains regardless of genuine quality improvement.
14	Given this caveat, the concrete benefit of adaptive $\bstar$ is operational: reducing grid search from nine runs to one (${\sim}$16 GPU-hours at 0.6B).
15	
16	\paragraph{Soft vs.\ hard filtering.}
17	At equal content epochs, D\&R ($17.657 \pm 0.006$) and adaptive $\bstar$ ($17.651 \pm 0.007$) are equivalent ($\Delta{=}0.006$, $N{=}3$); D\&R's full-length advantage (17.250 at $q{>}0.3$) requires ${\sim}$3.2$\times$ effective compute, and its U-shaped threshold curve is entirely a multi-epoch artifact (Figure~\ref{fig:dr_dual_curve}).

\paragraph{Why minimum intervention works.}
The $\aeff$ constraint prevents 4.9$\times$ over-aggressive downweighting in 38.2\% of batches (\S\ref{sec:regime}), with consistent behavior across $\rho$ and seeds (CV ${<}2\%$).
A fixed exponent at the aggregate mean $\bstar$ ($b{=}1.0$) yields PPL 17.692, indistinguishable from uniform (17.694): per-batch adaptation is essential, and the minimum intervention principle (adaptive, 17.651) outperforms maximum intervention (ESS-only, 17.738).

\paragraph{Failure modes and applicability boundary.}
At $\rho{=}0.2$, the method degrades by $+$0.046 PPL (Appendix~\ref{app:rho02}): the detector's mean $q$-score drops to 0.393, yet $\aeff$-binding rises to 60.1\%, so the method actively intervenes on unreliable signal.
The same pattern appears with generative detectors (GPT-2 PPL: $\Delta{=}{+}0.10$; N-gram PPL: $\Delta{=}{+}0.13$), which conflate predictability with provenance.
Both failure modes share a common root cause: when $q$-scores do not separate real from synthetic, the framework amplifies detector error rather than correcting for contamination.
The effective range with $\tau{=}0.8$ requires discriminative signal and $\rho \geq 0.4$.

\paragraph{Distribution matching, not quality gain.}
The in-distribution PPL improvement reverses out-of-distribution ($+$0.06 OpenWebText, $+$0.14 Wikipedia; seed 42, other-seed checkpoints not retained), consistent with distribution matching rather than general improvement.
This pattern likely affects all contamination-aware reweighting that upweights human-authored samples~\citep{drayson2025detection}: in-distribution PPL may be an inadequate metric for evaluating contamination mitigation, since any method that shifts the training distribution toward the evaluation distribution will show gains regardless of genuine quality improvement.
Given this caveat, the concrete benefit of adaptive $\bstar$ is operational: reducing grid search from nine runs to one (${\sim}$16 GPU-hours at 0.6B).

\paragraph{Soft vs.\ hard filtering.}
At equal content epochs, D\&R ($17.657 \pm 0.006$) and adaptive $\bstar$ ($17.651 \pm 0.007$) are equivalent ($\Delta{=}0.006$, $N{=}3$); D\&R's full-length advantage (17.250 at $q{>}0.3$) requires ${\sim}$3.2$\times$ effective compute, and its U-shaped threshold curve is entirely a multi-epoch artifact (Figure~\ref{fig:dr_dual_curve}).

\paragraph{Deployment considerations.}
$\tau{=}0.8$ is validated at $\rho{=}0.4$ (single-seed sweep) and $\rho{=}0.6$ ($\tau{=}0.7$ is optimal there); sensitivity at other contamination levels, model families, or corpus types is unknown (\S\ref{sec:limitations}).
Recommended defaults: discriminative detector with AUC ${\geq}$ 0.94, $\tau{=}0.8$, $\nmin{=}\lfloor B/2 \rfloor$.

\paragraph{Training Data.}
We sample a 132M-token subset of FineWeb~\citep{penedo2024fineweb} as the real-data source, comparable to typical domain-adaptive continued pretraining budgets~\citep{gururangan2020dont}.
To simulate web-scale synthetic contamination, we generate continuations with Qwen3-0.6B~\citep{yang2025qwen3}, the same architecture used for continued pretraining, and inject them at token-level ratio $\rho = 0.4$ via uniform random mixing.\footnote{$\rho$ denotes the token-level contamination ratio. Because synthetic documents are shorter on average (304 vs.\ 560 words), the document-level synthetic fraction is 55.6\% at $\rho{=}0.4$.}
This self-contamination design means generator and trainee share the same distribution; implications for detection difficulty are discussed in \S\ref{sec:limitations}.

\paragraph{Detector.}
We train a TF-IDF + Logistic Regression classifier on a held-out labeled split (AUC\,=\,0.94, calibrated ECE\,=\,0.05 after temperature scaling with $T{=}0.204$).
The resulting $q$-scores have mean 0.60, standard deviation 0.37, and median 0.71, with 46.3\% of samples in the uncertain range $[0.2, 0.8]$.
We use this lightweight detector rather than neural alternatives (e.g., ModernBERT at AUC\,${\geq}$\,0.98 in \citealt{drayson2025detection}) to test whether score \emph{calibration} may matter as much as raw discrimination for reweighting.
To evaluate detector sensitivity, we additionally test two generative baselines: a GPT-2-based perplexity scorer (AUC\,=\,0.913) and an N-gram language model perplexity scorer (AUC\,=\,0.73); results are reported in \S\ref{sec:robustness}.

\paragraph{Training.}
We continue pretraining Qwen3-0.6B from its pretrained weights for 6{,}103 steps (batch size 4, gradient accumulation 4, effective batch 16) with AdamW, cosine schedule (peak lr\,=\,$5{\times}10^{-5}$), max sequence length 2048, and bf16 precision on a single NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 (96\,GB).
All main comparisons use three random seeds (42, 123, 456).

\paragraph{Evaluation.}
We report held-out perplexity (PPL) on a held-out subset of FineWeb (67.8K documents, $\sim$4M tokens) containing only human-authored text, via sliding-window evaluation (stride 1024).
All evaluations are post-hoc with a unified pipeline; training involves no inline evaluation.

\paragraph{Methods.}
We compare six approaches:
\begin{itemize}[nosep,leftmargin=*]
  \item \textbf{Uniform}: $w_j = 1$ for all $j$ (no contamination handling).
  \item \textbf{Grid-$b$}: fixed $b \in \{0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.5, 1.0, 1.5, 2.0, 3.0, 5.0\}$ (nine candidates), best selected post-hoc by held-out PPL.
        Represents validation-based selection~\citep{drayson2025detection}.
  \item \textbf{ESS-only}: $b^* = \max\{b : \mathrm{ESS}(b) \geq n_{\min}\}$, the maximum-intervention variant retaining only the stability constraint, ablating $\alpha_{\mathrm{eff}}$.
  \item \textbf{Golden Ratio}: $w = 1/\varphi \approx 0.618$ for synthetic ($q_j > 0.5$), $w = 1$ otherwise~\citep{he2025golden}.
        Requires known provenance labels (oracle).
  \item \textbf{Adaptive} (ours): per-batch $b^*$ from the dual-constraint formulation (\S\ref{sec:method}), with $\tau = 0.8$ and $n_{\min} = 2$ (half the micro-batch size).
  \item \textbf{Detect \& Remove}: hard filtering that discards samples with $q_j > 0.5$ and trains uniformly on the remainder.
        Requires a calibrated detection threshold; threshold sensitivity is analyzed in \S\ref{sec:main-results}.
\end{itemize}

\paragraph{Training Data.}
We sample a 132M-token subset of FineWeb~\citep{penedo2024fineweb} as the real-data source, comparable to typical domain-adaptive continued pretraining budgets~\citep{gururangan2020dont}.
To simulate web-scale synthetic contamination, we generate continuations with Qwen3-0.6B~\citep{yang2025qwen3}, the same architecture used for continued pretraining, and inject them at token-level ratio $\rho = 0.4$ via uniform random mixing.\footnote{$\rho$ denotes the token-level contamination ratio. Because synthetic documents are shorter on average (304 vs.\ 560 words), the document-level synthetic fraction is 55.6\% at $\rho{=}0.4$.}
This self-contamination design means generator and trainee share the same distribution; implications for detection difficulty are discussed in \S\ref{sec:limitations}.

\paragraph{Detector.}
We train a TF-IDF + Logistic Regression classifier on a held-out labeled split (AUC\,=\,0.939, calibrated ECE\,=\,0.048 after temperature scaling with $T = 0.204$).
The resulting $q$-scores have mean 0.60, standard deviation 0.37, and median 0.71, with 46.3\% of samples in the uncertain range $[0.2, 0.8]$.
We use this lightweight detector rather than neural alternatives (e.g., ModernBERT at AUC\,${\geq}$\,0.98 in \citealt{drayson2025detection}) to test whether score \emph{calibration} may matter as much as raw discrimination for reweighting.
To evaluate detector sensitivity, we additionally test two generative baselines: a GPT-2-based perplexity scorer (AUC\,=\,0.913) and an N-gram language model perplexity scorer (AUC\,=\,0.73); results are reported in \S\ref{sec:robustness}.

\paragraph{Training.}
We continue pretraining Qwen3-0.6B from its pretrained weights for 6{,}103 steps (batch size 4, gradient accumulation 4, effective batch 16) with AdamW, cosine schedule (peak lr\,=\,$5{\times}10^{-5}$), max sequence length 2048, and bf16 precision on a single NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 (96\,GB).
All main comparisons use three random seeds (42, 123, 456).

\paragraph{Evaluation.}
We report held-out perplexity (PPL) on a held-out subset of FineWeb (67.8K documents, $\sim$4M tokens) containing only human-authored text, via sliding-window evaluation (stride 1024).
All evaluations are post-hoc with a unified pipeline; training involves no inline evaluation.

\paragraph{Methods.}
We compare six approaches:
\begin{itemize}[nosep,leftmargin=*]
  \item \textbf{Uniform}: $w_j = 1$ for all $j$ (no contamination handling).
  \item \textbf{Grid-$b$}: fixed $b \in \{0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.5, 1.0, 1.5, 2.0, 3.0, 5.0\}$ (nine candidates), best selected post-hoc by held-out PPL.
        Represents validation-based selection~\citep{drayson2025detection}.
  \item \textbf{ESS-only}: $b^* = \max\{b : \mathrm{ESS}(b) \geq n_{\min}\}$, the maximum-intervention variant retaining only the stability constraint, ablating $\alpha_{\mathrm{eff}}$.
  \item \textbf{Golden Ratio}: $w = 1/\varphi \approx 0.618$ for synthetic ($q_j > 0.5$), $w = 1$ otherwise~\citep{he2025golden}.
        Requires known provenance labels (oracle).
  \item \textbf{Adaptive} (ours): per-batch $b^*$ from the dual-constraint formulation (\S\ref{sec:method}), with $\tau = 0.8$ and $n_{\min} = 2$ (half the micro-batch size).
  \item \textbf{Detect \& Remove}: hard filtering that discards samples with $q_j > 0.5$ and trains uniformly on the remainder.
        Requires a calibrated detection threshold; threshold sensitivity is analyzed in \S\ref{sec:main-results}.
\end{itemize}
